<!-- thm-1: body_md -->
\label{T1.1} \cite[Proposition~1]{Carlet-JC-2025} For $0\le k\le n$, the function $f(X)=X^{2^k-1}$ defined on $\Bbb F_{2^n}$ is $k$th order sum-free.
<!-- end thm-1 -->
<!-- thm-2: body_md -->
\label{T1.2}
\cite[Theorem~ 5.1]{Hou-Zhao-FFA-2026} Assume $3\le k\le n-3$. If
\[
n\ge \frac{13}3k-1.37\quad\text{or}\quad n\le\frac{13}{10}k+0.41,
\]
$f_{\text{\rm inv}}$ is not $k$th order sum-free on $\Bbb F_{2^n}$.
<!-- end thm-2 -->
<!-- lem-1: body_md -->
\label{L2.1}
Let $m$ be a positive integer such that $\text{\rm wt}_q(m)\le k(q-1)$. Then
\[
\sum_{a_1,\dots,a_k\in\Bbb F_q}(Y+a_1X_1+\cdots+a_kX_k)^m=\sum_{a_1,\dots,a_k\in\Bbb F_q}(a_1X_1+\cdots+a_kX_k)^m.
\]
<!-- end lem-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
We have
\begin{align*}
&\sum_{a_1,\dots,a_k\in\Bbb F_q}(Y+a_1X_1+\cdots+a_kX_k)^m\cr
=\,&\sum_{a_1,\dots,a_k\in\Bbb F_q}\sum_{i_0,i_1,\dots,i_k}\binom m{i_0,i_1,\dots,i_k}Y^{i_0}(a_1X_1)^{i_1}\cdots(a_kX_k)^{i_k}\cr
=\,&\sum_{i_0,i_1,\dots,i_k}\binom m{i_0,i_1,\dots,i_k}Y^{i_0}X_1^{i_1}\cdots X_k^{i_k}\Bigl(\sum_{a_1\in\Bbb F_q}a_1^{i_1}\Bigr)\cdots\Bigl(\sum_{a_k\in\Bbb F_q}a_k^{i_k}\Bigr)\cr
=\,&(-1)^k\sum_{\substack{i_0,i_1,\dots,i_k\cr 0<i_j\equiv0\,(\text{mod}\, q-1),\,1\le j\le k}}\binom m{i_0,i_1,\dots,i_k}Y^{i_0}X_1^{i_1}\cdots X_k^{i_k}.
\end{align*}
In the above, $\binom m{i_0,i_1,\dots,i_k}\ne 0$ if and only if the sum $i_0+i_1+\cdots+i_k$ has no carries in base $p$ ($=\text{\rm char}\, \Bbb F_q$), hence only if $i_0+i_1+\cdots+i_k$ has no carries in base $q$. When $i_0+i_1+\cdots+i_k$ ($=m$) has no carries in base $q$, where $0<i_j\equiv 0\pmod{q-1}$ for $1\le j\le k$ and $\text{\rm wt}_q(m)\le k(q-1)$, we have $i_1+\cdots+i_k=m$, whence $i_0=0$. Therefore,
\[
\sum_{a_1,\dots,a_k\in\Bbb F_q}(Y+a_1X_1+\cdots+a_kX_k)^m=\sum_{a_1,\dots,a_k\in\Bbb F_q}(a_1X_1+\cdots+a_kX_k)^m.
\]
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lem-2: body_md -->
\label{L2.2}
Let $k$ be a positive integer. Then
\[
\sum_{a_1,\dots,a_k\in\Bbb F_q}(a_1X_1+\cdots+a_kX_k)^{q^k-1}=\prod_{0\ne(a_1,\dots,a_k)\in\Bbb F_q^k}(a_1X_1+\cdots+a_kX_k).
\]
<!-- end lem-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Let
\[
F(X_1,\dots,X_k)=\sum_{a_1,\dots,a_k\in\Bbb F_q}(a_1X_1+\cdots+a_kX_k)^{q^k-1},
\]
and treat it as a polynomial in $X_1$ over $\Bbb F_q[X_2,\dots,X_k]$. Let $\partial^iF$ denote the $i$th Hasse derivative of $F$ with respect to $X_1$ \cite[p.28]{Goldschmidt-2003}. For $0\le i<q-1$,
\[
\partial^iF=\binom{q^k-1}i\sum_{a_1,\dots,a_k\in\Bbb F_q}(a_1X_1+\cdots+a_kX_k)^{q^k-1-i}a_1^i.
\]
For $(b_2,\dots,b_k)\in\Bbb F_q^{k-1}$, we have
\begin{align*}
&\partial^iF\Bigm|_{X_1=-(b_2X_2+\cdots+b_kX_k)}\cr
=\,&\binom{q^k-1}i\sum_{a_1,\dots,a_k\in\Bbb F_q}\bigl((a_2-a_1b_2)X_2+\cdots+(a_k-a_1b_k)X_k\bigr)^{q^k-1-i}a_1^i\cr
=\,&\binom{q^k-1}i\sum_{a_2,\dots,a_k\in\Bbb F_q}(a_2X_2+\cdots+a_kX_k)^{q^k-1-i}\sum_{a_1\in\Bbb F_q}a_1^i\cr
=\,&0.
\end{align*}
Thus $-(b_2X_2+\cdots+b_kX_k)$ is a root of $F$ with multiplicity $\ge q-1$ \cite[Corollary~2.5.14]{Goldschmidt-2003}. Therefore
\begin{equation}\label{eq:|F}
\prod_{(a_1,\dots,a_k)\sim(1,b_2,\dots,b_k)}(a_1X_1+\cdots+a_kX_k)\mid F(X_1,\dots,X_k),
\end{equation}
where $(a_1,\dots,a_k)\sim(1,b_2,\dots,b_k)$ means that $(a_1,\dots,a_k)=u(1,b_2,\dots,b_k)$ for some $u\in\Bbb F_q^*$. Since $F(X_1,\dots,X_k)$ is symmetric in $X_1,\dots,X_k$, \eqref{eq:|F} implies that
\[
\prod_{0\ne(a_1,\dots,a_k)\in\Bbb F_q^k}(a_1X_1+\cdots+a_kX_k)\mid F(X_1,\dots,X_k).
\]
Comparing the degrees on both sides gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:c}
F(X_1,\dots,X_k)=c\prod_{0\ne(a_1,\dots,a_k)\in\Bbb F_q^k}(a_1X_1+\cdots+a_kX_k)
\end{equation}
for some $c\in\Bbb F_q$. The coefficient of $X_1^{(q-1)q^{k-1}}X_2^{(q-1)q^{k-2}}\cdots X_k^{(q-1)q^0}$ on the RHS of \eqref{eq:c} is
\[
c\Bigl(\prod_{a_1\in\Bbb F_q^*}a_1\Bigr)^{q^{k-1}}\cdots\Bigl(\prod_{a_k\in\Bbb F_q^*}a_k\Bigr)^{q^0}=c(-1)^k.
\]
The coefficient of $X_1^{(q-1)q^{k-1}}X_2^{(q-1)q^{k-2}}\cdots X_k^{(q-1)q^0}$ in $F(X_1,\dots,X_k)$ is 
\begin{align*}
&\sum_{a_1,\dots,a_k\in\Bbb F_q}\binom{q^k-1}{(q-1)q^{k-1},\dots,(q-1)q^0}a_1^{(q-1)q^{k-1}}\cdots a_k^{(q-1)q^0}\cr
=\,&\Bigl(\sum_{a_1\in\Bbb F_q}a_1^{q-1}\Bigr)^{q^{k-1}}\cdots\Bigl(\sum_{a_1\in\Bbb F_q}a_1^{q-1}\Bigr)^{q^0}=(-1)^k.
\end{align*}
Hence $c=1$.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- thm-3: body_md -->
\label{T2.3} ($q$-ary version of Theorem~\ref{T1.1}) For $0\le k\le n$, $f(X)=X^{q^k-1}$ is $k$th order sum-free on $\Bbb F_{q^n}$.
<!-- end thm-3 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Let $A$ be a $k$-dimensional $\Bbb F_q$-affine subspace of $\Bbb F_{q^n}$, and write $A=y+\langle u_1,\dots,u_k\rangle$, where $y\in\Bbb F_{q^n}$ and $u_1,\dots,u_k\in\Bbb F_{q^n}$ are linearly independent over $\Bbb F_q$. By Lemmas~\ref{L2.1} and \ref{L2.2},
\begin{align*}
\sum_{x\in A}f(x)\,&=\sum_{a_1,\dots,a_k\in\Bbb F_q}(y+a_1u_1+\cdots+a_ku_k)^{q^k-1}\cr
&=\prod_{0\ne(a_1,\dots,a_k)\in\Bbb F_q^n}(a_1u_1+\cdots+a_ku_k)\cr
&\ne 0.
\end{align*}
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- rmk-1: body_md -->
\label{R2.4}\rm
If $\text{\rm wt}_q(m)<k(q-1)$, it follows from the proof of Lemma~\ref{L2.1} that 
\[
\sum_{a_1,\dots,a_k\in\Bbb F_q}(Y+a_1X_1+\cdots+a_kX_k)^m=0.
\]
Hence every function $f:\Bbb F_{q^n}\to\Bbb F_{q^n}$ with algebraic degree $<k(q-1)$ is not $k$th order sum-free. (The algebraic degree of $f$ is the largest base $q$ weight of the degrees of the monomials in $f$.)
<!-- end rmk-1 -->
<!-- prop-1: body_md -->
\label{PA3}
Let $q$ be a prime power and $k, l$ be positive integers. Then
\begin{align}\label{eq:5}
&\Bigl(\sum_{a_1,\dots,a_k\in\Bbb F_q}(a_1X_1+\cdots+a_kX_k)^{(q-1)(1+q^l+q^{2l}+\cdots+q^{(k-1)l})} \Bigr)^{(q^l-1)/(q-1)}\\
&=\prod_{0\ne(b_1,\dots,b_k)\in\Bbb F_{q^l}^k}(b_1X_1+\cdots+b_kX_k).\nonumber
\end{align}
<!-- end prop-1 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Let
\[
F(X_1,\dots,X_k)=\sum_{a_1,\dots,a_k\in\Bbb F_q}(a_1X_1+\cdots+a_kX_k)^{(q-1)(1+q^l+q^{2l}+\cdots+q^{(k-1)l})},
\]
and treat it as a polynomial in $X_1$ over $\Bbb F_q[X_2,\dots,X_k]$. Let $\partial^iF$ be the $i$th Hasse derivative of $F$ with respect to $X_1$. For $0\le i<q-1$,
\[
\partial^iF=\binom{q-1}i \sum_{a_1,\dots,a_k\in\Bbb F_q}(a_1X_1+\cdots+a_kX_k)^{(q-1)(1+q^l+q^{2l}+\cdots+q^{(k-1)l})-i}a_1^i.
\]
For $(b_2,\dots,b_k)\in\Bbb F_{q^l}^{k-1}$, we have
\begin{align}\label{eq:6}
&\partial^iF\big|_{X_1=-(b_2X_2+\cdots+b_kX_k)}\\
=\,&\binom{q-1}i\sum_{a_1,\dots,a_k\in\Bbb F_q}\bigl((a_2-a_1b_2)X_2+\cdots+(a_k-a_1b_k)X_k\bigr)^{(q-1)(1+q^l+\cdots+q^{(k-1)l})-i}a_1^i\cr
=\,&\binom{q-1}i\sum_{a_1,\dots,a_k\in\Bbb F_q}\, a_1^i \bigl((a_2-a_1b_2)X_2+\cdots+(a_k-a_1b_k)X_k\bigr)^{q-1-i}\cr
&\kern8em\cdot \prod_{j=1}^{k-1}\bigl((a_2-a_1b_2)X_2^{q^{jl}}+\cdots+(a_k-a_1b_k)X_k^{q^{jl}}\bigr)^{q-1}.\nonumber
\end{align}
In the above,
\begin{align}\label{eq:7}
&a_1^i \bigl((a_2-a_1b_2)X_2+\cdots+(a_k-a_1b_k)X_k\bigr)^{q-1-i}\\
&\cdot\prod_{j=1}^{k-1}\bigl((a_2-a_1b_2)X_2^{q^{jl}}+\cdots+(a_k-a_1b_k)X_k^{q^{jl}}\bigr)^{q-1}\cr
=\,&\sum_{s_2+\cdots+s_k=k(q-1)-i}f_{s_2,\dots,s_k}(a_2-a_1b_2)^{s_2}\cdots(a_k-a_1b_k)^{s_k}a_1^i,\nonumber
\end{align}
where $f_{s_2,\dots,s_k}\in\Bbb F_q[X_2,\dots,X_k]$. Since $s_2+\cdots+s_k=k(q-1)-i>(k-1)(q-1)$, there exists $2\le i\le k$ such that $s_i\ge q$. For this $i$,
\[
(a_i-a_1b_i)^{s_i}=(a_i-a_1b_i)^q(a_i-a_1b_i)^{s_i-q}=(a_i-a_1b_i^q)(a_i-a_1b_i)^{s_i-q},
\]
where the total degree in $a_1,a_i$ on the RHS is $s_i-q+1$. Therefore, the product in \eqref{eq:7} can be expressed as a polynomial in $a_1,\dots,a_k$ with total degree $\le s_2+\cdots+s_k-q+1+i=(k-1)(q-1)<k(q-1)$. Then by \eqref{eq:6}, 
\[
\partial^iF\big|_{X_1=-(b_2X_2+\cdots+b_kX_k)}=0.
\]
Hence $(X_1+b_2X_2+\cdots+b_kX_k)^{q-1}\mid F(X_1,\dots,X_k)$. Since both sides of \eqref{eq:5} are symmetric in $X_1,\dots,X_k$, it follows that the RHS of \eqref{eq:5} divides the LHS. Comparing the total degrees (in $X_1,\dots,X_k$) on the two sides of \eqref{eq:5} gives 
\begin{align}\label{eq:8}
&\Bigl(\sum_{a_1,\dots,a_k\in\Bbb F_q}(a_1X_1+\cdots+a_kX_k)^{(q-1)(1+q^l+q^{2l}+\cdots+q^{(k-1)l})} \Bigr)^{(q^l-1)/(q-1)}\\
&=c\prod_{0\ne(b_1,\dots,b_k)\in\Bbb F_{q^l}^k}(b_1X_1+\cdots+b_kX_k)\nonumber
\end{align}
for some $c\in\Bbb F_{q^l}^*$.

The coefficient of $X_1^{(q^l-1)q^{(k-1)l}}X_2^{(q^l-1)q^{(k-2)l}}\cdots X_k^{(q^l-1)q^{0l}}$ on the RHS of \eqref{eq:8} is
\[
c\Bigl(\prod_{b_1\in\Bbb F_{q^l}^*}b_1\Bigr)^{q^{(k-1)l}}\cdots\Bigl(\prod_{b_b\in\Bbb F_{q^l}^*}b_k\Bigr)^{q^{0l}}=c(-1)^k.
\]
The coefficient of the same term on the LHS of \eqref{eq:8} is 
\begin{align}
&\sum_{a_1,\dots,a_k\in\Bbb F_q}a_1^{(q^l-1)q^{(k-1)l}}\cdots a_k^{(q^l-1)q^{0l}}\cr
=\,&\Bigl(\sum_{a_1\in\Bbb F_q}a_1^{q^l-1}\Bigr)^{q^{(k-1)l}}\cdots\Bigl(\sum_{a_k\in\Bbb F_q}a_k^{q^l-1}\Bigr)^{q^{0l}}=(-1)^k.
\end{align}
Hence $c=1$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- lem-3: body_md -->
\label{LA}
Let $m,n$ be positive integers such that $\gcd(m,n)=1$. If $u_1,\dots,u_k\in\Bbb F_{q^m}$ are linearly independent over $\Bbb F_q$, then they are also linearly independent over $\Bbb F_{q^n}$; that is, $\Bbb F_{q^m}$ and $\Bbb F_{q^n}$ are linearly disjoint over $\Bbb F_q$.
<!-- end lem-3 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Let $u_1,\dots,u_k\in\Bbb F_{q^m}$. By \cite[Lemma~2.30]{Hou-ams-gsm-2018}, $u_1,\dots,u_k$ are linearly independent over $\Bbb F_q$ if and only if
\begin{equation}\label{eq:1}
\text{\rm rank\,}\left[\begin{matrix}
u_1&\cdots&u_k\cr
u_1^q&\cdots&u_k^q\cr
\vdots&&\vdots\cr
u_1^{q^{m-1}}&\cdots&u_k^{q^{m-1}}
\end{matrix}
\right]=k.
\end{equation}
In the same way, $u_1,\dots,u_k$ are linearly independent over $\Bbb F_{q^n}$ if and only if
\begin{equation}\label{eq:2}
\text{\rm rank\,}\left[\begin{matrix}
u_1&\cdots&u_k\cr
u_1^{q^n}&\cdots&u_k^{q^n}\cr
\vdots&&\vdots\cr
u_1^{q^{n(m-1)}}&\cdots&u_k^{q^{n(m-1)}}
\end{matrix}
\right]=k.
\end{equation}
Since $\gcd(m,n)=1$, the matrix in \eqref{eq:2} is a row permutation of the matrix in \eqref{eq:1}. Hence \eqref{eq:1} and \eqref{eq:2} are equivalent.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- rmk-2: body_md -->
\label{R2.7}\rm
A more conceptual proof of Lemma~\ref{LA} is as follows: Put $\Bbb F_{q^m}$ and $\Bbb F_{q^n}$ in a fixed algebraic closure $\overline\Bbb F_q$. The $\Bbb F_q$-map $f:\Bbb F_{q^m}\otimes_{\Bbb F_q}\Bbb F_{q^n}\to \Bbb F_{q^m}[\Bbb F_{q^n}]=\Bbb F_{q^{mn}}$ sending $a\otimes b$ to $ab$ is onto. Since $\dim_{\Bbb F_q}\Bbb F_{q^m}\otimes_{\Bbb F_q}\Bbb F_{q^n}=mn=\dim_{\Bbb F_q}\Bbb F_{q^{mn}}$, $f$ is an $\Bbb F_q$-isomorphism. By \cite[Exercise~VI.2.1]{Hungerford-1980}, $\Bbb F_{q^m}$ and $\Bbb F_{q^n}$ are linearly disjoint over $\Bbb F_q$.
<!-- end rmk-2 -->
<!-- cor-1: body_md -->
\label{CA2}
Let $n,k,l$ be positive integers such that $2\le k\le n$. Then 
\[
X^{(q-1)(1+q^l+q^{2l}+\cdots+q^{(k-1)l})}
\]
is $k$th order sum-free if and only if $\gcd(l,n)=1$.
<!-- end cor-1 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
($\Leftarrow$) Let $A=y+\langle u_1,\dots,u_k\rangle$ be a $k$-dimensional $\Bbb F_q$-affine subspace of $\Bbb F_{q^n}$, where $u_1,\dots,u_k\in\Bbb F_{q^n}$ are linearly independent over $\Bbb F_q$ and $y\in\Bbb F_{q^n}$. By Lemma~\ref{LA}, $u_1,\dots,u_k$ are also linearly independent over $\Bbb F_{q^l}$. Then by Lemma~\ref{L2.1} and Proposition~\ref{PA3},
\[
\sum_{x\in A}x^{(q-1)(1+q^l+\cdots+q^{(k-1)l})}=\sum_{a_1,\dots,a_k\in\Bbb F_q}(a_1u_1+\cdots+a_ku_k)^{(q-1)(1+q^l+\cdots+q^{(k-1)l})}\ne0.
\]

\medskip
($\Rightarrow$) Assume to the contrary that $d=\gcd(l,n)>1$. Then there exist $u_1,\dots,u_k\in\Bbb F_{q^n}$ which are linearly independent over $\Bbb F_q$ but linearly dependent over $\Bbb F_{q^d}$. Then by Proposition~\ref{PA3},
\[
\sum_{a_1,\dots,a_k\in\Bbb F_q}(a_1u_1+\cdots+a_ku_k)^{(q-1)(1+q^l+\cdots+q^{(k-1)l})}=0,
\]
which is a contradiction.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- rmk-3: body_md -->
\label{R2.9}\rm
The binary form of Corollary~\ref{CA2} was stated in \cite[\S5.3]{Carlet-ePrint-2024} and a proof was outlined there. The proof of Corollary~\ref{CA2} given above is different.
<!-- end rmk-3 -->
<!-- lem-4: body_md -->
\label{L3.1}
$F_3(X_1,X_2,X_3)$ is absolutely irreducible, i.e., irreducible in $\overline\Bbb F_q[X_1,X_2,X_3]$.
<!-- end lem-4 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Since $F_3(X_1,X_2,X_3)$ is homogeneous, it suffices to show that $F_3(X_1,X_2,1)$ is absolutely irreducible. We have
\begin{align*}
&\Delta(X_1,X_2,1)=\left|\begin{matrix}
X_1&X_2&1\cr
X_1^q&X_2^q&1\cr
X_1^{q^2}&X_2^{q^2}&1
\end{matrix}\right|\cr
&=(X_1X_2^q-X_1^qX_2)-(X_1X_2^{q^2}-X_1^{q^2}X_2)+(X_1^qX_2^{q^2}-X_1^{q^2}X_2^q)\cr
&=X_1X_2\bigl[(X_2^{q-1}-X_1^{q-1})-(X_2^{q^2-1}-X_1^{q^2-1})+(X_1^{q-1}X_2^{q^2-1}-X_1^{q^2-1}X_2^{q-1})\bigr],
\end{align*}

\begin{align*}
&\Delta_1(X_1,X_2,1)=\left|\begin{matrix}
X_1&X_2&1\cr
X_1^{q^2}&X_2^{q^2}&1\cr
X_1^{q^3}&X_2^{q^3}&1
\end{matrix}\right|\cr
&=(X_1X_2^{q^2}-X_1^{q^2}X_2)-(X_1X_2^{q^3}-X_1^{q^3}X_2)+(X_1^{q^2}X_2^{q^3}-X_1^{q^3}X_2^{q^2})\cr
&=X_1X_2\bigl[(X_2^{q^2-1}-X_1^{q^2-1})-(X_2^{q^3-1}-X_1^{q^3-1})+(X_1^{q^2-1}X_2^{q^3-1}-X_1^{q^3-1}X_2^{q^2-1})\bigr].
\end{align*}
Write
\[
F_3(X_1,X_2,1)=C_{q^2-q}+C_{q^2-q+1}+\cdots+C_{q^3-q},
\]
where $C_i\in\Bbb F_q[X_1,X_2]$ is homogeneous of degree $i$. Then 
\begin{align}\label{eq:C+...}
&(C_{q^2-q}+\cdots+C_{q^3-q})\Bigl(1-\frac{X_2^{q^2-1}-X_1^{q^2-1}}{X_2^{q-1}-X_1^{q-1}}+\frac{X_1^{q-1}X_2^{q^2-1}-X_1^{q^2-1}X_2^{q-1}}{X_2^{q-1}-X_1^{q-1}}\Bigr)\\
&=\frac{X_2^{q^2-1}-X_1^{q^2-1}}{X_2^{q-1}-X_1^{q-1}}-\frac{X_2^{q^3-1}-X_1^{q^3-1}}{X_2^{q-1}-X_1^{q-1}}+\frac{X_1^{q^2-1}X_2^{q^3-1}-X_1^{q^3-1}X_2^{q^2-1}}{X_2^{q-1}-X_1^{q-1}}.\nonumber
\end{align}
Comparing the homogeneous parts of the two sides of \eqref{eq:C+...} gives
\[
C_{q^2-q}=\frac{X_2^{q^2-1}-X_1^{q^2-1}}{X_2^{q-1}-X_1^{q-1}},
\]
and for $q^2-q<i<q^3-q$, 
\[
C_i-C_{i-(q^2-q)}\frac{X_2^{q^2-1}-X_1^{q^2-1}}{X_2^{q-1}-X_1^{q-1}}+C_{i-(q^2-1)}\frac{X_1^{q-1}X_2^{q^2-1}-X_1^{q^2-1}X_2^{q-1}}{X_2^{q-1}-X_1^{q-1}}=0,
\]
where $C_j$ is defined as 0 for $j<q^2-q$. Using induction on $i$ we see that 
\[
C_{q^2-q}=\frac{X_2^{q^2-1}-X_1^{q^2-1}}{X_2^{q-1}-X_1^{q-1}}\,\Big |\, C_i\quad\text{for all}\ q^2-q\le i<q^3-q.
\]
We also have
\[
C_{q^3-q}=\frac{X_1^{q^2-1}X_2^{q^3-1}-X_1^{q^3-1}X_2^{q^2-1}}{X_1^{q-1}X_2^{q^2-1}-X_1^{q^2-1}X_2^{q-1}}.
\]
By Eisenstein's criterion, $F_3(X_1,X_2,1)$ is absolutely irreducible if we can show that $C_{q^2-q}$ is separable and $\gcd(C_{q^2-q},C_{q^3-q})=1$, equivalently, $C_{q^2-q}(1,X_2)$ is separable and 
\[
\gcd\bigl(C_{q^2-q}(1,X_2),C_{q^3-q}(1,X_2)\bigr)=1.
\]
Since $X_2(X_2^{q^2-1}-1)=X_2^{q^2}-X_2$ is separable, it follows that 
\[
C_{q^2-q}(1,X_2)=\frac{X_2^{q^2-1}-1}{X_2^{q-1}-1}
\]
is separable. We also have
\begin{align*}
&\gcd\bigl(C_{q^2-q}(1,X_2),C_{q^3-q}(1,X_2)\bigr)\cr
=\,&\gcd\Bigl(\frac{X_2^{q^2-1}-1}{X_2^{q-1}-1},\,\frac{X_2^{q^3-1}-X_2^{q^2-1}}{X_2^{q^2-1}-X_2^{q-1}}\Bigr)\cr
\,\Big|\,&\gcd\Bigl(\frac{X_2^{q^2-1}-1}{X_2^{q-1}-1},\,\frac{X_2^{q^3-1}-X_2^{q^2-1}}{X_2^{q-1}-1}\Bigr)\cr
=\,&\frac 1{X_2^{q-1}-1}\gcd(X_2^{q^2-1}-1,\,X_2^{q^3-1}-X_2^{q^2-1})\cr
=\,&\frac 1{X_2^{q-1}-1}\gcd(X_2^{q^2-1}-1,\,X_2^{q^3-1}-1)\cr
=\,&\frac 1{X_2^{q-1}-1}\gcd(X_2^{\gcd(q^2-1,q^3-1)}-1)=1.
\end{align*}
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- lem-5: body_md -->
\label{L3.2}
For $k\ge 3$, $F_k(X_1,\dots,X_k)$ has an absolutely irreducible factor in $\Bbb F_q[X_1,\dots,X_k]$.
<!-- end lem-5 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
We use induction on $k$. When $k=3$, by Lemma~\ref{L3.1}, $F_3(X_1,X_2,X_3)$ is absolutely irreducible.

Now assume $k>3$. It suffices to show that $F_k(X_1,\dots,X_{k-1},1)$ has an absolutely irreducible factor in $\Bbb F_q[X_1,\dots,X_k]$. Write
\[
F_k(X_1,\dots,X_{k-1},1)=\frac{\Delta_1(X_1,\dots,X_{k-1},1)}{\Delta(X_1,\dots,X_{k-1},1)}=C_{q^{k-1}-q}+C_{q^{k-1}-q+1}+\cdots,
\]
where $C_i\in\Bbb F_q[X_1,\dots,X_{k-1}]$ is homogeneous of degree $i$ and 
\[
C_{q^{k-1}-q}=\frac{\Delta_1(X_1,\dots,X_{k-1})}{\Delta(X_1,\dots,X_{k-1})}=F_{k-1}(X_1,\dots,X_{k-1}).
\]
By the induction hypothesis, $C_{q^{k-1}-q}$ has an absolutely irreducible factor $h\in\Bbb F_q[X_1,\dots,X_{k-1}]$. For $1\le i\le k-1$,
\[
\frac{\partial}{\partial X_i}\Delta_1(X_1,\dots,X_{k-1})=\pm\Delta(X_1,\dots,X_{i-1},X_{i+1},\dots,X_{k-1})^{q^2},
\]
which is nonzero and independent of $X_i$. Hence $\Delta_1(X_1,\dots,X_{k-1})$ is separable in each $X_i$, so $\Delta_1(X_1,\dots,X_{k-1})$ is square-free. It follows that $h^2\nmid C_{q^{k-1}-q}$. Now by \cite[Lemma~1.11]{Sze-Thesis-2023}, $F_k(X_1,\dots,X_{k-1},1)$ has an absolutely irreducible factor in $\Bbb F_q[X_1,\dots,X_{k-1}]$.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- head-1: body_md -->
We believe that $F_k(X_1,\dots,X_k)$ ($k\ge 3$) itself is absolutely irreducible. However, having an absolutely irreducible factor in $\Bbb F_q[X_1,\dots,X_k]$ is enough for the purpose of the following theorem.
<!-- end head-1 -->
<!-- thm-4: body_md -->
\label{T3.3} ($q$-ary version of Theorem~\ref{T1.2}) Assume $3\le k\le n-3$. If
\[
n\ge\frac{13}3k+2\log_q\frac 12(1+\sqrt{21})
\]
or
\[
n\le\frac{13}{10}k-\frac35\log_q\frac 12(1+\sqrt{21}),
\]
$g_{q-1}$ is not $k$th order sum-free on $\Bbb F_{q^n}$.
<!-- end thm-4 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
By the statement before Lemma~\ref{L3.1}, to prove that $g_{q-1}$ is not $k$th order sum-free on $\Bbb F_{q^n}$, it suffices to show that 
\[
\bigl|V_{\Bbb F_{q^n}^k}(F_k)\setminus V_{\Bbb F_{q^n}^k}(\Delta)\bigr|>0.
\]
Since $F_k$ has an absolutely irreducible factor $h\in\Bbb F_q[X_1,\dots,X_k]$ (Lemma~\ref{L3.2}), by the Lang-Weil bound as stated in \cite[Theorem~5.2]{Cafure-Matera-FFA-2006}, we have
\begin{align}\label{eq:LW}
&|V_{\Bbb F_{q^n}^k(}(F_k)|\ge|V_{\Bbb F_{q^n}^k}(h)|\\
&\ge q^{n(k-1)}-(q^k-q-1)(q^k-q-2)q^{n(k-3/2)}-5(q^k-q)^{13/3}q^{n(k-2)}\cr
&>q^{n(k-1)}-q^{2k}q^{n(k-3/2)}-5q^{13k/3}q^{n(k-2)}\cr
&=q^{n(k-2)}\bigl[q^n-q^{2k}q^{n/2}-5q^{13k/3}\bigr].\nonumber
\end{align}
Since $\Delta_1(X_1,\dots,X_k)$ is square-free, we have $\gcd(F_k,\Delta)=1$. Hence by \cite[Lemma~2.2]{Cafure-Matera-FFA-2006}
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Bezout}
\bigl|V_{\Bbb F_{q^n}^k}(F_k)\cap V_{\Bbb F_{q^n}^k}(\Delta)\bigr|\le\max\{\deg F_k,\,\deg\Delta\}^2q^{n(k-2)}\le q^{2k}\cdot q^{n(k-2)}.
\end{equation}
Combining \eqref{eq:LW} and \eqref{eq:Bezout} gives
\[
\bigl|V_{\Bbb F_{q^n}^k}(F_k)\setminus V_{\Bbb F_{q^n}^k}(\Delta)\bigr|>q^{n(k-2)}\bigl[q^n-q^{2k}q^{n/2}-5q^{13k/3}-q^{2k}\bigr].
\]
Let $x_0$ denote the larger root of the quadratic $X^2-q^{2k}X-5q^{13k/3}-q^{2k}\in\Bbb R[X]$.Then
\begin{align*}
x_0\,&=\frac 12\bigl[q^{2k}+(q^{4k}+20q^{13k/3}+4q^{2k})^{1/2}\bigr]\cr
&\le\frac 12\bigl[q^{2k}+(21q^{13k/3})^{1/2}\bigr]\cr
&\le\frac 12(1+\sqrt{21})q^{13k/6}.
\end{align*}
When $q^{n/2}\ge x_0$, i.e., when
\[
n\ge\frac{13}3k+2\log_q\frac 12(1+\sqrt{21}),
\]
we have 
\[
\bigl|V_{\Bbb F_{q^n}^k}(F_k)\setminus V_{\Bbb F_{q^n}^k}(\Delta)\bigr|>0,
\]
whence $g_{q-1}$ is not $k$th order sum-free on $\Bbb F_{q^n}$.

Since $g_{q-1}$ is $k$th order sum-free on $\Bbb F_{q^n}$ if and only if it is $(n-k)$-th order sum-free on $\Bbb F_{q^n}$, when 
\[
n\ge\frac{13}3(n-k)+2\log_q\frac 12(1+\sqrt{21}),
\]
i.e., when
\[
n\le\frac{13}{10}k-\frac35\log_q\frac 12(1+\sqrt{21}),
\]
$g_{q-1}$ is not $k$th order sum-free on $\Bbb F_{q^n}$ neither.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- thm-5: body_md -->
\label{t4.1}\cite{Carlet-2021, Carlet-Charpin-Zinoviev-DCC-1998}
For $n\ge 4$, a function $f:\Bbb F_{2^n}\to \Bbb F_{2^n}$ is APN if and only if $C(f)$ is a $[2^n,2^n-2n-1,6]$ code.
<!-- end thm-5 -->
<!-- rmk-4: body_md -->
\label{r4.2}\rm
Theorem~\ref{t4.1} was proved, in an equivalent form, by Carlet, Charpin and Zinoviev \cite{Carlet-Charpin-Zinoviev-DCC-1998}, and was stated in the present form in \cite{Carlet-2021}. It is not difficult to see that $f$ is APN if and only if $C(f)$ is a $[2^n,k,d]$ code with $k\ge 2^n-2n-1$ and $d\ge 6$. The sphere packing bound shows that $d\le 6$, and by a result of \cite{Brouwer-Tolhuizen-DCC-1993}, we have $k\le 2^n-2n-1$.

When $n=3$, $f:\Bbb F_{2^3}\to\Bbb F_{2^3}$ is APN if and only if $C(f)$ is an $[8,1,8]$ code.
<!-- end rmk-4 -->
<!-- thm-6: body_md -->
\label{t4.3}\cite[Theorem~1]{Kasami-Tokura-IEEE-IT-1970} For $0<r\le n$, the next-to-minimum weight of $R(r,n)$ is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:2wt}
2^{n-r}+c 2^{n-r-1},
\end{equation}
where $2^{n-r}$ is the minimum weight of $R(r,n)$ and
\[
c=\begin{cases}
2&\text{if}\ r=1,\cr
1&\text{if}\ 2\le r\le n-2,\cr
2&\text{if}\ r=n-1,n.
\end{cases}
\]
<!-- end thm-6 -->
<!-- thm-7: body_md -->
\label{t4.4}\cite[Theorem~4.5]{Bruen-CM523-2010} \cite[Theorem~3.1]{Erickson-thesis-1974}
Assume $q>2$, and let $0<r\le n(q-1)$, written in the form $r=s(q-1)+t$, $0<t\le q-1$. Then the next-to-minimum weight of $R_q(r,n)$ is 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:2wtq}
(q-t)q^{n-s-1}+cq^{n-s-2},
\end{equation}
where $(q-t)q^{n-s-1}$ is the minimum weight of $R_q(r,n)$ and
\[
c=\begin{cases}
q&\text{if}\ s=n-1,\cr
t-1&\text{if}\ s\le n-2,\ t>1\cr
q&\text{if}\ 0<s\le n-2,\ q\ge 4,\ t=1,\cr
q-1&\text{if}\ 0<s\le n-2,\ q=3,\ t=1,\cr
q&\text{if}\ s=0,\ t=1.
\end{cases}
\]
<!-- end thm-7 -->
<!-- thm-8: body_md -->
\label{t4.5}
Assume $q=2$ and $1\le s\le n-1$. A function $f:\Bbb F_{2^n}\to \Bbb F_{2^n}$ is $s$th order sum-free if and only if $C_s(f)$ is a $[2^n,k,d]$ code over $\Bbb F_2$ with
\begin{equation}\label{eq:k-ge}
k\ge 2^n-n-\sum_{i=0}^{s-1}\binom ni,
\end{equation}
\begin{equation}\label{eq:d-ge}
d\ge\begin{cases}
4&\text{if}\ s=1,\cr
2^s+2^{s-1}&\text{if}\ 2\le s\le n-2,\cr
2^n&\text{if}\ s=n-1.
\end{cases}
\end{equation}
<!-- end thm-8 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
\eqref{eq:k-ge} is obvious. Since $R(s-1,n)^\bot=R(n-s,n)$, we have
\[
C_s(f)=\{u\in R(n-s,n): (f(x_0),\dots,f(x_{q^n-1}))u^T=0\}.
\]
The right side of $\eqref{eq:d-ge}$ is the next-to-minimum weight of $R(n-s,n)$. Therefore,
\begin{align*}
&\text{\eqref{eq:d-ge} holds}\cr
\Leftrightarrow\ &\text{for each minimum weight codeword $u\in R(n-s,n)$},\cr
&(f(x_0),\dots,f(x_{2^n-1}))u^T\ne 0,\cr
\Leftrightarrow\ & \text{for each indicator vector $u$ of an $s$-dimensional $\Bbb F_2$-affine subspace of $\Bbb F_{2^n}$},\cr
&(f(x_0),\dots,f(x_{2^n-1}))u^T\ne 0,\cr
\Leftrightarrow\ & \sum_{x\in A}f(x)\ne 0\ \text{for every $s$-dimensional $\Bbb F_2$-affine subspace $A$ of $\Bbb F_{2^n}$},\cr
\Leftrightarrow\ &\text{$f$ is $s$th order sum-free}.
\end{align*}
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- thm-9: body_md -->
\label{t4.6}
Assume $q>2$ and $1\le s\le n-1$. A function $f:\Bbb F_{q^n}\to\Bbb F_{q^n}$ is $s$th order sum-free if and only if $C_s(f)$ is a $[q^n,k,d]$ code over $\Bbb F_q$ with
\begin{equation}\label{eq:qk-ge}
k\ge q^n-n-\dim_{\Bbb F_q}R_q(s(q-1)-1,n),
\end{equation}
\begin{equation}\label{eq:qd-ge}
d\ge q^s+(q-2)q^{s-1}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end thm-9 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
The proof is identical to that of Theorem~\ref{t4.5}. We only have to note that the right side of \eqref{eq:qd-ge} is the next-to-minimum weight of $R_q(s(q-1)-1,n)^\bot=R_q((n-s)(q-1),n)$ and that the minimum weight codewords of $R_q((n-s)(q-1),n)$ are indicator vectors of $s$-dimensional $\Bbb F_q$-affine subspaces of $\Bbb F_{q^n}$.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- rmk-5: body_md -->
\label{R4.7}\rm
As we mentioned in the introduction, Theorem~\ref{t4.5} was covered by the main result of \cite{Heering-Kaspers-Taranchuk-2026}. When $f:\Bbb F_{2^n}\to\Bbb F_{2^n}$ is $s$th order sum-free with $2\le s\le n-2$, it was also proved in \cite{Heering-Kaspers-Taranchuk-2026} that the minimum weight of $C_s(f)$ is $3\cdot 2^{s-1}$. Theorem~\ref{t4.6} is new to our best knowledge.
<!-- end rmk-5 -->
<!-- rmk-6: body_md -->
\label{R4.1}\rm
The above proof is essentially based on the same idea as the proof in \cite{Dobbertin-IC-1999}. What differs the two proofs is in their approaches to polynomial equations over finite fields. The proof of \cite{Dobbertin-IC-1999} relied on clever trace arguments. Our strategy is to reduce polynomial equations continuously using resultants, hiding the subtleties behind computations. Our approach can be placed in the framework of a more general algebraic question.
<!-- end rmk-6 -->
<!-- ques-1: body_md -->
\label{Q4.2}\rm
Let $\Bbb F$ be a field and $I$ an ideal of $\Bbb F[X_1.\dots,X_k]$ with the following properties:
\begin{itemize}
\item[(i)] $I$ contains one or several given polynomials.

\item[(ii)] If $g,h\in\Bbb F[X_1,\dots,X_k]$ are such that $gh\in I$, then either $g\in I$ or $h\in I$. ($I$ is not necessarily a prime ideal because it could be the entire ring $\Bbb F[X_1,\dots,X_k]$.)

\item[(iii)] There exists $\sigma=(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_k)\in\Bbb F[X_1,\dots,X_k]^k$ such that $g\in I$ implies $g\circ\sigma\in I$.
\end{itemize}
The objective is to find a few elements in $\Bbb F[X_1,\dots,X_k]$, with degrees as low as possible, such that $I$ contains at least one of them.
<!-- end ques-1 -->
<!-- thm-10: body_md -->
\label{T4.3}\cite[Theorem~2.29]{Hou-ams-gsm-2018}
For $a_0,\dots,a_{n-1}\in\Bbb F_{q^n}$, the roots of the $q$-polynomial $a_0X+a_1X^q+\cdots+a_{n-1}X^{q^{n-1}}$ in $\Bbb F_{q^n}$ is a vector space over $\Bbb F_2$ of dimension $n-\text{\rm rank\,}\mathcal D(a_0,\dots,a_{n-1})$.
<!-- end thm-10 -->
<!-- defn-1: body_md -->
\label{D4.4} For an $m\times n$ matrix $A$, a set of rows with indices $i,i+1,\dots,i+k \pmod m$ is called a set of {\em continuous rows}. A set of continuous columns is defined the same way. A {\em continuous submatrix} of $A$ is a submatrix whose row indices are $i,i+1,\dots,i+k \pmod m$ and whose column indices are $j,j+1,\dots,j+l \pmod n$.
<!-- end defn-1 -->
<!-- lem-6: body_md -->
\label{L4.5}
Let $A$ be an $n\times n$ Dickson matrix over $\Bbb F_{q^n}$ with $\text{\rm rank\,} A=r$. Then any set of $r$ continuous rows (columns) are linearly independent over $\Bbb F_{q^n}$.
<!-- end lem-6 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Write
\[
A=\left[\begin{matrix} w_1\cr\vdots\cr w_n\end{matrix}\right].
\]
Assume to the contrary and without loss of generality that $w_1,\dots,w_r$ are linearly dependent over $\Bbb F_{q^n}$. Then there exists $s\le r$ such that $w_s$ is a linear combination of $w_1,\dots,w_{s-1}$, say
\[
w_s=b_1w_1+\cdots+b_{s-1}w_{s-1},\quad b_i\in\Bbb F_{q^n}.
\]
Apply $(\ )^q$ to the components of both sides of the above equation. We have
\begin{align*}
w_{s+1}\,&=b_1^qw_2+\cdots+b_{s-2}^qw_{s-1}+b_{s-1}^qw_s\cr
&=b_{s-1}^qb_1w_1+(b_{s-1}^qb_2+b_1^q)w_2+\cdots+(b_{s-1}^qb_{s-1}+b_{s-2}^q)w_{s-1}\cr
&\in\langle w_1,\dots,w_{s-1}\rangle.
\end{align*}
Continuing this way, we see that $w_i\in\langle w_1,\dots,w_{s-1}\rangle$ for all $s\le i\le n$. Then $\text{\rm rank\,} A\le s-1$, which is a contradiction.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- cor-2: body_md -->
\label{C4.6}
Let $A$ be an $n\times n$ Dickson matrix over $\Bbb F_{q^n}$ with $\text{\rm rank\,} A=r$. Then every $r\times r$ continuous submatrix of $A$ is nonsingular.
<!-- end cor-2 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
Without loss of generality, we only prove that the $r\times r$ leading principal submatrix of $A$ is nonsingular. Write
\[
A=[c_1,\dots,c_n].
\]
By Lemma~\ref{L4.5}, $\text{\rm rank\,}[c_1,\dots,c_r]=r$, and the first $r$ rows of $[c_1,\dots,c_r]$ span the row space of $[c_1,\dots,c_r]$. Therefore, the $r\times r$ leading principal submatrix of $A$, which consists of the first $r$ rows of $[c_1,\dots,c_r]$, is nonsingular.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- prop-2: body_md -->
\label{P4.7}
Let $A$ be an $n\times n$ Dickson matrix over $\Bbb F_{q^n}$. Then the following statements are equivalent:
\begin{itemize}
\item[(i)] $\text{\rm rank\,} A=r$.

\item[(ii)] All $r\times r$ continuous submatrices of $A$ are nonsingular, and for each $r<i\le n$, all $i\times i$ submatrices of $A$ are singular.

\item[(iii)] $A$ has an $r\times r$ nonsingular submatrix, and for each $r<i\le n$, $A$ has an $i\times i$ singular continuous submatrix.
\end{itemize}
<!-- end prop-2 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
(i) $\Rightarrow$ (ii). This is Corollary~\ref{C4.6}.

\medskip
(ii) $\Rightarrow$ (i) Obvious.

\medskip
(ii) $\Rightarrow$ (iii). Obvious.

\medskip
(iii) $\Rightarrow$ (i). By Corollary~\ref{C4.6}, $\text{\rm rank\,} A\ne i$ for all $r<i\le n$. On the other hand, we clearly have $\text{\rm rank\,} A\ge r$.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- thm-11: body_md -->
\label{T4.8}
Let $n\ge 5$ and let $D^*(x)$ denote the leading $(n-2)\times(n-2)$ principal submatrix of the Dickson matrix $D(x)$ in \eqref{eq:D(x)}. Then the Welch function $W_n(X)$ on $\Bbb F_{2^n}$ is not 3rd order sum-free if and only if $\det D^*(x)=0$ for some $x\in\Bbb F_{2^n}\setminus\Bbb F_2$.
<!-- end thm-11 -->
<!-- cor-3: body_md -->
\label{C4.9}
The Welch function $W_n(X)$ on $\Bbb F_{2^n}$ ($n\ge 5$) is not 3rd order sum-free if and only if 
\begin{equation}\label{eq:deggcd}
\deg\gcd(\det D^*(X),\,X^{2^n}+X)>2.
\end{equation}
<!-- end cor-3 -->
<!-- conj-1: body_md -->
\label{C4.10}
For $n=2m+1\ge 7$, the Welch function on $\Bbb F_{2^n}$ is not $3$rd order sum-free.
<!-- end conj-1 -->
<!-- conj-2: body_md -->
\label{C5.11}
For $0<i_1<i_2<n$, the function $f_{n,i_1,i_2}(X)$ is $3$rd order sum-free on $\Bbb F_{2^n}$ if and only if $\{0,i_1,i_2\}\overset n\sim\{0,1,2\}$.
<!-- end conj-2 -->
